title: Ankle Dorsiflexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit on the floor with one leg straight out in front of you (long-sit).
• Keep your knee straight (soft, not locked) and toes pointing up toward the ceiling.
• Sit tall through your spine; if hamstrings are tight, sit on a folded towel or bend the other knee for comfort.
• Keep the working leg’s heel on the floor and the toes relaxed (not gripping).
Movement
1. Pull your toes toward your shin (like you’re trying to show the bottom of your foot forward).
2. Focus on moving at the ankle joint—not by curling the toes.
3. Pause for 1–2 seconds at the top.
4. Slowly return to neutral (don’t point the toes unless instructed).
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per side
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Feel the work in the front of the shin (tibialis anterior), not in the toes.
• Keep the knee straight and the heel grounded.
• Move slow and controlled—no snapping
videoDescription: This drill improves ankle dorsiflexion (toes up), which supports better squatting, walking, and stair mechanics. Keep the heel down, lift from the ankle (not the toes), and move with control.

title: Ankle Plantar Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit on the floor with one leg straight out in front of you (long-sit).
• Keep the knee straight but not locked; toes relaxed.
• Sit tall through your spine. If hamstrings are tight, sit on a folded towel.
• Keep the working leg’s heel on the floor.
Movement
1. Slowly point your toes away from your shin (press the “gas pedal”).
2. Focus on moving at the ankle joint—don’t curl the toes hard.
3. Pause for 1–2 seconds at the end range.
4. Return to neutral with control (don’t snap back).
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per side
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Move from the ankle (foot points), not aggressive toe curling.
• Keep the knee straight and relaxed.
• Slow and controlled both directions.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Toe gripping/cramping → point less, keep toes long, slow down.
• Knee bending → gently straighten; sit on a towel if needed.
• Snapping fast → control the return.
videoDescription: Plantar flexion is pointing your foot away from your shin (like pressing a gas pedal). This drill strengthens the calf/ankle connection and improves push-off mechanics for walking, stairs, running, and jumping—while keeping it low-impact and easy to control

title: Elbow Extension
instructions:
Setup / Posture:

• Sit or stand upright with your spine tall and core engaged

• Begin with your elbow bent and hand near your shoulder

• Keep the upper arm stationary close to the body
Movement:

• Slowly straighten the elbow, extending your hand downward until the arm is fully extended

• Avoid locking out the elbow forcefully

• Pause briefly at the end, then return to the bent position under control
Reps / Sets:

• Perform 10–15 repetitions

• Complete 2–3 sets

• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:

• Builds strength in the triceps and supports joint stability

• Balances muscle engagement in the upper arm

• Enhances pushing ability and functional arm movement
videoDescription: This video demonstrates elbow extension—straightening the arm from a bent position. Begin with the elbow bent at a 90-degree angle. Slowly extend the arm until it is fully straight, then return with control. This movement builds strength in the back of the arm and supports pushing movements in daily life and upper body workouts.

title: Elbow Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture:

• Sit or stand upright with your shoulders back and down

• Keep your arms relaxed by your sides, elbows extended

• Palms can face forward (supinated), inward (neutral), or downward (pronated) depending on variation
Movement:

• Slowly bend the elbow, bringing your hand toward your shoulder

• Keep your upper arm still — only the forearm should move

• Pause briefly at the top, then slowly lower back to the start
Reps / Sets:

• Perform 10–15 repetitions

• Complete 2–3 sets

• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:

• Strengthens the biceps and surrounding elbow flexors

• Improves upper limb coordination and grip-related tasks

• Beneficial for restoring strength imbalances and joint control
videoDescription: his video demonstrates elbow flexion—the bending of the elbow to bring the forearm toward the upper arm. Stand or sit with arms by your sides and palms facing forward. Slowly bend the elbow while keeping your upper arm stationary, then return to the starting position. This movement strengthens the front of the arm and improves functional movement patterns for daily tasks.

title: Finger Abduction & Adduction
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit or stand comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Hold one hand out in front of you at chest height, palm facing forward (or rest your forearm on a table).
• Keep your wrist neutral (not bent up or down).
• Relax your fingers—no tension in the knuckles.
Movement
1. Abduction (Open): Slowly spread your fingers apart as wide as you can without strain.
2. Pause for 1–2 seconds at the widest point.
3. Adduction (Close): Slowly bring your fingers back together until they touch lightly.
4. Keep the motion smooth and controlled—avoid snapping.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 open/close reps per hand
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of slow, smooth reps
Focus
• Move from the fingers (not the wrist).
• Keep fingers long—avoid curling or clawing.
• Smooth control both directions; light effort, not force.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Wrist bending or moving → Rest forearm on a table; keep wrist neutral.
• Fingers curling/clawing → “Keep fingers long; spread from the base of the fingers.”
• Tension in shoulders/neck → Drop shoulders; breathe slowly.
videoDescription: Finger abduction and adduction are the motions of spreading your fingers apart and bringing them back together. This drill improves hand control and coordination, which supports daily tasks like typing, gripping, writing, lifting, and fine motor work—especially when hands feel stiff or weak.

title: Finger Extension
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit or stand comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Rest your forearm on a table or hold your hand out in front of you.
• Start with your hand relaxed, palm facing down or forward.
• Keep your wrist neutral (not bent up or down).
Movement
1. Begin with fingers gently relaxed (slightly bent is fine).
2. Slowly straighten and lengthen your fingers, opening the hand as if you’re making a flat palm.
3. Pause 1–2 seconds at full extension (without forcing).
4. Return to the relaxed start position with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per hand
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Keep the motion in the fingers (don’t let the wrist lead).
• Extend the fingers long—avoid locking or snapping.
• Light tension is okay; avoid sharp pain.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Wrist bends up → Rest forearm on a table; keep wrist neutral.
• Fingers hyperextend/lock → “Straighten long, not hard.”
• Shoulders tense → Drop shoulders and breathe slowly.
videoDescription: Finger extension is the motion of straightening your fingers and opening the hand. This drill improves hand control and tendon glide, supporting daily activities like typing, gripping, lifting, writing, and opening jars, especially if your hands feel stiff from overuse or screen time.

title: Finger Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit or stand comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Rest your forearm on a table or hold your hand out in front of you.
• Keep your wrist neutral (not bent up or down).
• Start with fingers straight and relaxed.
Movement
1. Slowly bend your fingers and close your hand into a gentle fist.
2. Aim to wrap the fingers smoothly—avoid squeezing hard.
3. Pause 1–2 seconds in the fist.
4. Slowly open the hand back to the start position with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per hand
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Keep the movement smooth (no snapping).
• Make a gentle fist—this is coordination/mobility unless you’re specifically strengthening.
• Keep wrist neutral and shoulders relaxed.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Squeezing too hard → “Gentle fist, light effort.”
• Wrist bends → Rest forearm on table; keep wrist neutral.
• Finger joints collapse/awkward → Slow down and close the hand in stages (tips → middle → base).
videoDescription: Finger flexion is the motion of bending your fingers to grip (closing the hand). This drill supports daily tasks like holding objects, carrying bags, lifting, writing, and opening containers by improving hand coordination and tendon glide—especially if your hands feel stiff or weak.

title: Forearm Pronation
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit or stand comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Bend your elbow to about 90 degrees and keep it close to your side.
• Start with your palm facing up or neutral (thumb-up).
• Keep your wrist straight and relaxed (don’t bend it).
Movement
1. Slowly rotate your forearm so your palm turns downward.
2. Pause 1–2 seconds at the end range.
3. Slowly rotate back to the starting position with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per side
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth rotations
Focus
• Rotate from the forearm—keep the upper arm still.
• Keep the wrist neutral (avoid bending or flicking).
• Smooth, controlled movement; stay pain-free.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Elbow drifting away from side → Tuck a towel between elbow and ribs.
• Wrist bending → “Keep your wrist straight; rotate from the forearm.”
• Shoulder rotating → Keep shoulder relaxed; move only the forearm.
videoDescription: Forearm pronation is the motion of rotating your forearm so your palm faces down. This movement is used constantly in daily life—typing, pushing doors, using tools, lifting objects, and most gym grips—and helps maintain healthy wrist and elbow mechanics.

title: Forearm Supnation
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit or stand comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Bend your elbow to about 90 degrees and keep it close to your side.
• Start with your palm facing down or neutral (thumb-up).
• Keep your wrist straight and relaxed (don’t bend it).
Movement
1. Slowly rotate your forearm so your palm turns upward.
2. Pause 1–2 seconds at the end range.
3. Slowly rotate back to the starting position with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per side
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth rotations
Focus
• Rotate from the forearm—keep the upper arm still.
• Keep the wrist neutral (avoid bending or flicking the hand).
• Smooth and controlled; stay pain-free.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Elbow drifting away from side → Tuck a towel between elbow and ribs.
• Wrist bending → “Keep knuckles in line with forearm.”
• Shoulder rotating → Keep shoulder relaxed; move only the forearm.
videoDescription: Forearm supination is the motion of rotating your forearm so your palm faces up (like holding a bowl of soup). This movement supports daily tasks like turning a key, opening a door knob, carrying a tray, using tools, and many gym grips, and helps maintain healthy wrist/elbow mechanics.

title: Hip Extension
instructions:
Setup / Posture:

• Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor

• Arms relaxed at your sides, core gently engaged
Movement:

• Press through your heels and lift your hips toward the ceiling, squeezing your glutes at the top

• Keep ribs down and avoid arching your lower back

• Pause at the top, then lower with control
Reps / Sets:

• Perform 10–12 reps

• Complete 2–3 sets
Focus:

• Strengthens glutes and hamstrings for postural balance

• Reduces excessive lumbar extension (helps correct pelvic tilt)

• Reinforces proper hip hinge mechanics for lifts and daily movements
videoDescription: Hip extension builds strength and stability through the posterior chain. This is crucial for correcting anterior pelvic tilt, improving posture, and preventing low back pain.

title: Hip Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture:

• Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat (or seated upright)

• Maintain a neutral spine with rib cage down and core engaged
Movement:

• Lift one knee toward your chest, keeping the pelvis stable

• Do not arch your back or twist your hips — isolate the motion from the hip joint

• Lower slowly and repeat on the other side
Reps / Sets:

• Perform 8–10 reps per leg

• Complete 2–3 sets
Focus:

• Strengthens and activates the hip flexors in isolation

• Helps identify imbalance or compensation from the lumbar spine

• Supports functional movements like walking and stair climbing
videoDescription: Hip flexion is a foundational movement that supports walking, squatting, and core control. This version teaches mindful activation without compensating from the lower back.

title: Mandible Depression
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand upright with good posture:
    ◦ Spine tall, shoulders relaxed
    ◦ Head aligned over shoulders (not jutting forward)
    ◦ Tongue relaxed and resting on the floor of your mouth
• Eyes forward, jaw relaxed — do not clench your teeth.
Movement:
1. Begin the Depression:
    ◦ Slowly open your mouth by lowering your jaw in a straight, controlled motion.
    ◦ Try to keep the motion smooth and centered — avoid the jaw shifting side to side.
    ◦ Open to a comfortable range (about halfway to full open), stopping before any pain or joint clicking.
2. Return to Start:
    ◦ Close your mouth gently and completely without clenching your teeth together.
    ◦ Maintain a relaxed facial expression throughout.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 slow, controlled reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest briefly between sets if needed
Focus:
• Improves mobility in the temporomandibular joint (TMJ)
• Strengthens the muscles responsible for controlled mandible (jaw) movement
• Reduces jaw tension and supports posture by relaxing associated neck/jaw muscles
• Beneficial for clients with TMJ tension, forward head posture, or excessive jaw clenching
videoDescription: This video teaches mandible depression, or how to properly lower the jaw to help relieve tension and improve TMJ mobility. Begin with an upright posture, neck aligned, and lips gently closed. Slowly open your mouth by lowering your jaw without jutting it forward. Focus on a smooth motion downward and avoid tension in the neck. Pause at the bottom, then return with control.

title: Mandible Elevation
instructions:
etup / Posture:
• Sit or stand upright with your spine tall and shoulders relaxed
• Head in a neutral position over the shoulders
• Mouth gently open in a relaxed state, jaw centered (not shifted to one side)
• Avoid clenching or tensing neck or facial muscles
Movement:
1. Begin the Elevation:
    ◦ Slowly close your mouth by raising the jaw upward in a smooth, controlled motion
    ◦ Bring the bottom teeth toward the top teeth without snapping or clenching
    ◦ Focus on keeping the jaw centered (avoid sideways movement)
2. Return to Start:
    ◦ Pause gently with lips together, then reopen to the relaxed start position
    ◦ Avoid tensing your tongue or facial muscles throughout the movement
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 slow, controlled reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest briefly between sets if needed
Focus:
• Strengthens masseter, temporalis, and other jaw-closing muscles
• Improves control and function of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ)
• Helps reduce jaw fatigue or overuse tension from excessive talking, chewing, or clenching
• Complements jaw-opening (mandible depression) exercises for balanced TMJ health
videoDescription: This video demonstrates mandible elevation, or controlled jaw closing. Begin with your mouth open slightly in a relaxed position and head upright. Slowly close your jaw by bringing the lower jaw upward until the teeth are gently together. Emphasize smooth movement using the muscles of the jaw, not the neck. This helps with bite alignment and TMJ stability.

title: Mandible Lateral Deviation
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand upright with your spine aligned and shoulders relaxed
• Keep your head level and facing forward — avoid turning or tilting
• Lips gently closed, teeth slightly apart, and jaw relaxed
Movement:
1. Glide to One Side:
    ◦ Slowly move your lower jaw to the right side, aiming to shift the bottom teeth slightly past the top teeth on that side
    ◦ Keep the movement horizontal — avoid tilting, jutting, or rotating the head or neck
    ◦ You should feel gentle activation in the jaw muscles on the shifting side
2. Return to Center:
    ◦ Slowly bring your jaw back to the neutral position
3. Glide to the Other Side:
    ◦ Repeat the same movement to the left, keeping it smooth and controlled
    ◦ Then return to center
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 8–10 reps per side
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest briefly between sets
Focus:
• Activates and balances the pterygoid muscles, masseter, and temporalis
• Improves jaw symmetry, motor control, and reduces clenching or grinding patterns
• Supports alignment and mobility of the TMJ, especially beneficial for clients with jaw tension, headaches, or upper-crossed syndrome
videoDescription: This video demonstrates how to perform mandible lateral deviation—moving your jaw side to side. Begin seated or standing tall with good posture. Slowly shift your lower jaw to the right without turning your head, then return to center and repeat to the left. This movement helps improve jaw mobility and balance between sides, especially helpful for those with jaw tension or TMJ dysfunction.

title: Mandible Protraction
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand upright with your spine neutral and shoulders relaxed
• Keep your head level, ears aligned over shoulders (avoid tilting or jutting the chin upward)
• Begin with the jaw relaxed, lips gently closed but not clenched
Movement:
1. Glide Forward:
    ◦ Slowly slide your lower jaw forward so that your bottom teeth move in front of your top teeth
    ◦ Keep the movement horizontal — do not tilt the head or open the mouth wide
    ◦ Focus on control and avoid any jerky movement
2. Return to Start:
    ◦ Gently return the jaw to its natural resting position
    ◦ Keep facial muscles relaxed throughout
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 slow, controlled reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest as needed between sets
Focus:
• Activates and strengthens lateral pterygoid and digastric muscles involved in forward jaw motion
• Improves function and mobility of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ)
• Helpful in balancing muscle activity in clients with postural jaw issues or clenching habits
• Supports alignment correction for forward head posture by retraining jaw awareness and control
videoDescription: This video shows how to perform mandible protraction—sliding the lower jaw forward. Start seated or standing tall with a neutral head position. Without tilting the head, slowly move your jaw straight forward, like you’re making an underbite. Pause briefly, then return to the starting position. This improves jaw control and mobility, helpful for TMJ health.

title: Mandible Retraction
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand tall with your spine straight and shoulders relaxed
• Keep your head level with ears aligned over shoulders
• Relax your jaw with your lips gently closed and teeth not clenched
Movement:
1. Glide Backward:
    ◦ Gently pull your lower jaw straight back, aiming to align your bottom teeth directly beneath or slightly behind your top teeth
    ◦ Do not tilt the head or tuck the chin—only the jaw should move
    ◦ Move slowly and in control, avoiding jerking or clenching
2. Return to Start:
    ◦ Glide the jaw forward back to its natural resting position
    ◦ Keep the neck and face relaxed throughout
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 slow, controlled reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest briefly between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens and trains the temporalis, masseter, and deep cervical stabilizers
• Improves temporomandibular joint (TMJ) function and helps counter jaw protrusion habits
• Supports postural alignment in clients with forward head posture, helping bring awareness and balance to the head and neck relationship
videoDescription: Learn how to perform mandible retraction, or pulling the jaw backward. Sit or stand upright. Begin with a relaxed jaw, then gently draw your lower jaw back—like making a “double chin” with the jaw—not the neck. Focus on the backward glide of the jaw, pause, then return forward. Great for posture correction and jaw alignment.

title: Neck Circles
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand tall with a neutral spine and shoulders relaxed away from your ears.
• Keep your core gently engaged and your head aligned directly over your shoulders.
• Maintain a calm, steady breath to stay relaxed through the motion.
Movement:
1. Start Center:
    ◦ Begin with your head in a neutral position, eyes looking forward.
2. Circle Clockwise:
    ◦ Slowly lower your chin toward your chest.
    ◦ Gently begin to circle your head to the right, bringing your right ear toward your right shoulder.
    ◦ Continue the motion by tilting your head back into a gentle extension (looking up), then rolling your left ear toward your left shoulder.
    ◦ Complete the circle by returning your chin to your chest.
3. Pause and Reverse:
    ◦ Perform the same movement in the opposite (counterclockwise) direction.
    ◦ Move slowly and smoothly without jerking or forcing the motion.
    ◦ Keep your shoulders relaxed and avoid shrugging.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 3–5 slow circles in each direction
• Complete 2 sets
• Breathe steadily throughout
Focus:
• Increases mobility and circulation in the neck and upper spine
• Gently releases tight neck muscles and improves body awareness
• Supports reduction of neck stiffness and forward head posture over time
videoDescription: This video demonstrates full-range neck circles to gently mobilize the neck and improve flexibility in all directions. You'll be guided through a smooth, slow rotation with mindful control to reduce stiffness and improve neck health. Great for warm-ups or decompressing after long days.

title: Neck Flexion & Extension
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand tall with your spine upright and shoulders relaxed.
• Ears should be stacked directly over your shoulders (avoid slouching or chin jutting forward).
• Engage your core slightly to support your spine. Keep hands relaxed at your sides or resting gently on your lap.
Movement:
1. Flexion (Chin to Chest):
    ◦ Slowly lower your chin toward your chest in a controlled motion.
    ◦ Feel a gentle stretch in the back of the neck.
    ◦ Pause at the bottom for 1–2 seconds without forcing the stretch.
2. Extension (Look Up):
    ◦ Reverse the motion by gently lifting your chin upward toward the ceiling.
    ◦ Keep your shoulders down and avoid arching your back.
    ◦ Pause when you feel a stretch in the front of your neck—don’t strain or overextend.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 8–10 slow, controlled reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Breathe steadily throughout the movement
Focus:
• This exercise improves neck mobility and posture awareness.
• Helps relieve tension from poor posture (like forward head) and long hours sitting or looking down.
videoDescription: This video guides you through controlled neck flexion and extension to improve mobility, posture, and relieve tension. Learn how to align your spine, engage your core, and move the neck safely through full forward and backward motion without compensation from the shoulders or low back.

title: Neck Lateral Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand tall with your spine upright and shoulders relaxed.
• Stack your ears directly over your shoulders and keep your chin level (avoid letting the head drift forward).
• Engage your core slightly to support posture. Hands can rest comfortably at your sides or on your lap.
Movement:
1. Side Bend (Right):
    ◦ Slowly tilt your right ear toward your right shoulder without lifting the shoulder or rotating the head.
    ◦ Keep your face pointing forward and your chest tall.
    ◦ Pause for 1–2 seconds when you feel a gentle stretch along the side of your neck.
2. Return to Center:
    ◦ Slowly bring your head back to the neutral center position with control.
3. Side Bend (Left):
    ◦ Tilt your left ear toward your left shoulder, maintaining relaxed shoulders and upright posture.
    ◦ Pause for 1–2 seconds at the end range without forcing the stretch.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 8–10 slow reps per side
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Move with controlled breathing throughout
Focus:
• Improves side-to-side neck mobility and posture alignment.
• Helps reduce neck stiffness, tension headaches, and muscle imbalance from forward head or shoulder posture.
videoDescription: This movement helps gently stretch and strengthen the muscles on the sides of your neck. The video will teach you how to tilt your ear toward your shoulder without lifting your shoulder, while maintaining an upright posture. Great for relieving tension and increasing neck mobility.
otherNames: Neck Side Flexion | Neck Side Bend | Neck Tilt

title: Neck Rotation
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand tall with your spine neutral and shoulders relaxed down and back.
• Keep your chin level and head stacked directly over your shoulders (not jutting forward).
• Lightly engage your core to stabilize your upper body.
Movement:
1. Rotate Right:
    ◦ Slowly turn your head to the right, as if you're looking over your shoulder.
    ◦ Keep your chin level (avoid tipping it up or down).
    ◦ Move only your head — keep your shoulders still and relaxed.
    ◦ Stop when you feel a comfortable stretch without strain and pause for 1–2 seconds.
2. Return to Center:
    ◦ Bring your head back to the neutral position with control.
3. Rotate Left:
    ◦ Repeat the movement by turning your head to the left.
    ◦ Pause again for 1–2 seconds at the end range.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 8–10 reps per side
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Breathe steadily and move slowly throughout the motion
Focus:
• Improves cervical spine rotation and joint mobility
• Helps relieve neck tension, correct posture imbalances, and support healthy head positioning for those with forward head posture
videoDescription: In this exercise, you’ll learn how to rotate your head left and right with control and proper posture. This video helps improve range of motion, release neck stiffness, and promote better alignment—especially helpful for desk workers and those with upper body tension.

title: Rib Elevation & Depression
instructions:
Setup / Posture:

• Sit upright or lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat

• Spine should be neutral with shoulders relaxed away from ears

• Place hands lightly on your lower rib cage or sides of the torso to feel the rib movement

• Keep your jaw relaxed and lips gently closed
Movement:
1. Rib Elevation (Inhalation):

• Inhale deeply through your nose, focusing on expanding your rib cage outward and upward

• Allow the ribs to lift and widen without lifting the shoulders or arching the back

• You should feel your ribs pressing gently into your hands
2. Rib Depression (Exhalation):

• Exhale slowly through pursed lips

• As you exhale, draw the ribs downward and inward, engaging the abdominals

• Think of your ribs knitting together toward your center without collapsing your chest
Reps / Sets:

• Perform 6–10 slow and controlled full breath cycles

• Complete 2–3 rounds, resting between rounds if needed
Focus:

• Improves diaphragm activation and respiratory efficiency

• Supports spinal and thoracic mobility

• Reinforces core control and posture, especially helpful for clients with rib flare, upper-crossed syndrome, or shallow breathing habits
videoDescription: This exercise helps retrain proper breathing mechanics and improve thoracic mobility. By practicing rib elevation and depression with control, clients learn how to use their diaphragm effectively, reduce tension in accessory muscles, and support better posture and core engagement.

title: Scapula Depression
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand upright with a tall spine, chest lifted slightly, and shoulders relaxed.
• Keep your arms hanging by your sides or hold light resistance (e.g., dumbbells) if appropriate.
• Engage your core to stabilize your torso and avoid arching your lower back.
Movement:
1. Start Position:
    ◦ Begin with your shoulders in a neutral resting position (not shrugged or pulled down).
2. Depress Shoulders:
    ◦ Slowly draw your shoulder blades downward toward your back pockets.
    ◦ Think about lengthening your neck and moving your shoulders away from your ears.
    ◦ Hold the depressed position briefly (1–2 seconds) while keeping your arms relaxed.
3. Return to Neutral:
    ◦ Slowly release the shoulder blades back to the starting position without shrugging.
    ◦ Avoid using your arms to pull the shoulders down — the movement should come from your scapular muscles.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens the lower trapezius and stabilizing muscles of the scapula
• Reduces overactivation of the upper traps, helping correct shoulder elevation
• Supports posture correction for clients with forward head and upper-crossed syndrome
videoDescription: earn how to perform scapula depression to activate the muscles that pull your shoulder blades down and away from your ears. This movement is key for improving posture, reducing upper trap dominance, and creating more control around your shoulders. Great for people with forward head posture or neck tension.

title: Scapula Downward Rotation
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand tall with feet hip-width apart or sit upright on a bench.
• Begin with arms overhead, biceps near the ears, elbows slightly bent (in a "Y" position).
• Core engaged, ribs down, and neck relaxed.
• Chin tucked gently to maintain neutral spine and reduce forward head posture.
Movement:
1. Start Position:
    ◦ From the overhead "Y" position, begin pulling your elbows down and back toward your sides (like a lat pulldown).
    ◦ Imagine squeezing your shoulder blades downward and inward toward your back pockets.
2. Engage the Scapula:
    ◦ Focus on moving the shoulder blades down and in, initiating the motion from the scapula, not the arms.
    ◦ Avoid shrugging or using the upper traps.
3. Return to Start:
    ◦ Slowly raise your arms back to the overhead "Y" position, feeling the scapula rotate upward with control.
    ◦ Maintain core engagement and a neutral head position throughout.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens the rhomboids, levator scapulae, and latissimus dorsi
• Reinforces healthy scapular motion and stability
• Supports correction of rounded shoulders and improves posture
videoDescription: This video demonstrates scapula downward rotation—drawing the shoulder blades downward and inward. It helps strengthen the stabilizers of the upper back and shoulders and balances muscles involved in posture and shoulder positioning.

title: Scapula Elevation
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand or sit tall with your spine neutral, chest slightly lifted, and arms relaxed by your sides.
• Maintain a long neck (ears stacked over shoulders) and gently engage your core.
• You may hold light dumbbells if appropriate for added resistance or simply use bodyweight for mobility activation.
Movement:
1. Start Position:
    ◦ Begin with shoulders resting in a neutral position — not pulled down or elevated.
2. Elevate Shoulders:
    ◦ Slowly lift both shoulders straight upward toward your ears in a smooth, controlled motion.
    ◦ Avoid rolling the shoulders forward or backward — the movement should go straight up.
    ◦ Pause at the top for 1–2 seconds, feeling a gentle squeeze in the upper trapezius.
3. Return to Start:
    ◦ Lower your shoulders slowly back to the neutral position.
    ◦ Keep the movement controlled and avoid letting the shoulders drop quickly.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–45 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Activates and strengthens the upper trapezius
• Improves mind-muscle awareness of shoulder movement
• Can be used to balance over-depressed scapulae or promote full range of scapular control (when used intentionally in corrective sequences)
videoDescription: This video teaches proper scapula elevation to help you understand how to lift your shoulder blades upward in a controlled and isolated motion. This is helpful for reconnecting with shoulder mechanics, building awareness of overactive upper traps, and setting a foundation for shoulder stability exercises.

title: Scapula Protraction
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand or sit upright with a neutral spine and relaxed shoulders.
• Extend both arms straight in front of you at chest height, palms facing down (as if reaching forward).
• Keep a slight bend in the elbows and engage your core to avoid arching the low back.
• Focus on keeping the neck relaxed and head stacked over the shoulders.
Movement:
1. Start Position:
    ◦ Begin with your shoulder blades (scapulae) gently pulled back and down in a neutral position.
2. Protract (Reach Forward):
    ◦ Slowly push your arms forward by gliding your shoulder blades away from your spine.
    ◦ Think about spreading your upper back — your arms move slightly forward, but the movement comes from the scapulae, not just the arms.
    ◦ You should feel a stretch between the shoulder blades and engagement in the serratus anterior muscles along the side of the ribs.
3. Return to Start:
    ◦ Slowly retract your shoulder blades to the neutral position.
    ◦ Avoid shrugging or bending the elbows.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–45 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens the serratus anterior
• Improves scapular mobility and control
• Helps counteract poor posture caused by winging or underactive stabilizers
• Supports shoulder stability during pressing and overhead movements
videoDescription: This video teaches how to properly perform scapula protraction — a foundational movement for shoulder stability and posture correction. Learn how to glide your shoulder blades forward along the rib cage without shrugging or bending the arms. Ideal for beginners, corrective exercise, and building a strong foundation for pressing movements.

title: Scapula Retraction
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Sit or stand tall with a neutral spine.
• Arms extended straight in front of you at shoulder height, palms facing down.
• Engage your core to keep your torso stable.
• Keep the neck relaxed and chin gently tucked to align head over shoulders.
Movement:
1. Start Position:
    ◦ Begin with arms straight and shoulder blades in a neutral position (not pinched or spread).
2. Retract (Pull Back):
    ◦ Pull your shoulder blades back toward your spine without bending your elbows.
    ◦ Think about squeezing a pencil between your shoulder blades.
    ◦ Keep shoulders down and away from the ears to avoid using the upper traps.
    ◦ This movement is small but controlled — the arms move slightly as a result of scapular motion.
3. Return to Start:
    ◦ Slowly release back to the neutral position.
    ◦ Avoid shrugging or flaring the ribs.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–45 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens the middle trapezius and rhomboids
• Improves posture and mid-back activation
• Helps correct rounded shoulders by increasing scapular stability
• Prepares the upper body for pulling movements like rows or pull-ups
videoDescription: This video walks you through scapula retraction—pulling the shoulder blades back toward the spine. This movement strengthens postural muscles and helps reverse rounded shoulders from sitting or slouching. Perfect for improving upper back strength, posture correction, and shoulder stability.

title: Scapula Upward Rotation
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand tall with feet hip-width apart.
• Hold light dumbbells or no weight at all (based on client level).
• Start with arms down at your sides, palms facing your body.
• Engage your core, keep spine neutral, and relax your neck and traps.
• Chin tucked slightly to keep head aligned over shoulders.
Movement:
1. Start Position:
    ◦ Bring both arms up and out in a "Y" motion (similar to a shoulder raise but at a 45° angle from your torso).
    ◦ Elbows stay straight or soft (do not lock), and wrists stay neutral.
2. Rotate and Lift:
    ◦ As you raise your arms, think about your shoulder blades rotating upward and outward, wrapping slightly around the ribcage.
    ◦ Avoid shrugging the shoulders — the movement comes from the scapula rotating, not elevation of the traps.
    ◦ Pause briefly at the top without arching the lower back.
3. Lower with Control:
    ◦ Slowly lower the arms back to the start position, maintaining control.
    ◦ Focus on controlled scapular movement — no momentum.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Activates the serratus anterior, lower trapezius, and upper trapezius in balance
• Encourages healthy shoulder blade motion necessary for overhead activities
• Helps correct shoulder dysfunction and supports better posture in upper crossed syndrome
videoDescription: Learn how to perform scapula upward rotation—an essential movement for healthy shoulder mechanics and overhead motion. This video shows how to activate and control the upward movement of your shoulder blades, promoting strength and mobility in the upper back and shoulders.

title: Shoulder Abduction
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand tall with feet hip-width apart or sit upright on a bench or chair.
• Engage your core by gently bracing your midsection and drawing your ribs down.
• Arms should rest at your sides with palms facing the thighs.
• Maintain a neutral spine, chin tucked slightly, and shoulders relaxed (not shrugged).
Movement:
1. Begin the Abduction:
    ◦ Slowly raise both arms straight out to the sides until they reach shoulder height (or as high as your mobility allows without compensation).
    ◦ Keep your elbows straight and palms facing the floor.
    ◦ Do not lean or arch your back — only your arms should be moving.
2. Pause and Control:
    ◦ Briefly hold at the top with shoulder blades gently stabilized.
    ◦ Avoid shrugging shoulders or elevating traps.
3. Return to Start:
    ◦ Lower the arms back down slowly and with control.
    ◦ Reset posture if needed between reps.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens middle deltoids and rotator cuff stabilizers
• Improves shoulder mobility and postural awareness
• Supports healthy movement mechanics for overhead reaching and arm control
videoDescription: This video demonstrates shoulder abduction—raising your arm out to the side and up. You’ll learn how to keep proper alignment and avoid shoulder shrugging. Useful for building shoulder strength and improving range of motion for daily tasks and overhead lifts.

title: Shoulder Adduction
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand tall or sit upright on a bench/chair with feet planted.
• Keep your spine neutral, chin slightly tucked, and shoulders relaxed.
• Arms start raised at shoulder height, extended out to the sides (like a "T" shape), palms facing downward or slightly forward.
• Engage your core to maintain upright posture and avoid arching your back.
Movement:
1. Begin the Adduction:
    ◦ Slowly lower both arms down toward your sides, bringing them back to your torso in a controlled motion.
    ◦ Focus on moving only through the shoulder joint, keeping arms straight and avoiding excessive momentum.
2. Pause and Control:
    ◦ Briefly pause when your arms return to your sides.
    ◦ Keep shoulder blades gently stabilized and avoid letting them roll forward.
3. Return to Start (if repeating dynamically):
    ◦ Raise the arms back out to shoulder height with control if performing for reps.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens and activates latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, and teres major
• Promotes control of shoulder motion and supports postural balance
• Complements shoulder abduction by training the opposite movement
videoDescription: Learn how to perform shoulder adduction by bringing your arm back down toward your side from an outstretched position. This movement helps improve control, posture, and strengthens the pulling muscles of the upper body.

title: Shoulder Extension
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand tall with feet hip-width apart or sit upright on a bench or chair.
• Keep core braced, ribs drawn down, chin slightly tucked, and shoulders relaxed away from ears.
• Arms start straight at your sides, palms facing your thighs or slightly behind, depending on range of motion.
• Maintain a neutral spine — avoid arching your low back.
Movement:
1. Begin the Extension:
    ◦ Slowly move both arms straight behind you as far as comfortable without bending the elbows.
    ◦ Keep your palms facing in or slightly back depending on shoulder comfort.
    ◦ Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades slightly together as arms extend.
2. Control the Motion:
    ◦ Move only through the shoulder joint — avoid arching your back or swinging.
    ◦ Keep neck and traps relaxed.
3. Return to Start:
    ◦ Slowly bring your arms back to the starting position at your sides with control.
    ◦ Reset posture if needed between reps.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens the posterior deltoids, triceps, and upper back stabilizers
• Improves posture by activating muscles that oppose forward shoulder rounding
• Encourages mobility and strength in the shoulder girdle
videoDescription: Watch how to perform shoulder extension by moving the arm straight back. This simple movement improves shoulder mobility, posture, and engages key back and arm muscles needed for pulling strength and posture correction.

title: Shoulder External Rotation
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand tall or sit upright with feet flat on the floor.
• Maintain a neutral spine, engage your core, and gently pull shoulder blades back and down.
• Bend your elbow at 90 degrees, upper arm close to your torso, forearm parallel to the floor and pointing forward.
• This can be done using a resistance band, light dumbbell, or cable machine for added resistance.
Movement:
1. Begin the Rotation:
    ◦ With your elbow fixed at your side, rotate your forearm outward, away from your body.
    ◦ Keep your upper arm stable—only your forearm should move.
    ◦ Focus on control and avoid twisting your torso or lifting the shoulder.
2. Return to Start:
    ◦ Slowly rotate your arm back to the starting position, maintaining tension and control.
    ◦ Avoid letting the arm "snap" back—stay smooth and steady.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps per arm
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens the infraspinatus and teres minor muscles
• Supports rotator cuff health and shoulder joint stability
• Helps improve posture by countering forward shoulder rotation (common in upper crossed syndrome)
videoDescription: This video demonstrates shoulder external rotation to activate the back of the shoulder and rotator cuff. Start with your elbow bent at 90 degrees and close to your side, forearm across your stomach. Rotate the forearm outward, keeping the elbow in place, until your forearm is pointing to the side. Slowly return to the starting position. Keep your core engaged and shoulders relaxed throughout the movement.

title: Shoulder Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand tall with feet hip-width apart or sit upright on a bench or chair.
• Keep your shoulders stacked over hips, core braced, ribs down, and chin gently tucked.
• Arms start by your sides with palms facing in toward your body.
• Maintain neutral spine and avoid leaning back as you lift.
Movement:
1. Initiate the Lift:
    ◦ Slowly raise both arms straight forward and up in front of you until they reach shoulder height or slightly higher (no higher than ear level).
    ◦ Keep elbows extended but not locked, and maintain thumbs-up position if needed for shoulder comfort.
2. Controlled Movement:
    ◦ Focus on lifting from the shoulders (not shrugging).
    ◦ Avoid arching the low back — keep your core engaged and spine neutral.
3. Lower with Control:
    ◦ Slowly lower your arms back to your sides with control.
    ◦ Reset posture between reps as needed.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens the anterior deltoids and supports mobility of the shoulder joint
• Encourages proper scapular rhythm and upper-body posture
• Helps correct forward-rounded shoulders when performed with good alignment
videoDescription: This video demonstrates shoulder flexion—lifting the arm forward and up. You'll learn how to control the movement with proper posture and alignment. Great for improving overhead reach, shoulder strength, and upper body function.

title: Shoulder Horizontal Abduction
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Begin standing or seated upright on a bench/chair with feet grounded.
• Maintain a tall spine, core engaged, and shoulders down and back.
• Raise your arms straight out in front of you at shoulder height, palms facing each other (neutral grip).
• Keep a soft bend in your elbows throughout the movement.
Movement:
1. Begin the Abduction:
    ◦ Open your arms outward to the sides in a wide arc (as if opening your arms to give a hug), keeping them at shoulder height.
    ◦ Squeeze your shoulder blades together as you move, ensuring the movement comes from the shoulders—not the spine.
    ◦ Pause when your arms are directly out to the sides (forming a "T" position).
2. Return to Start:
    ◦ Slowly bring your arms back to the starting position in front of you.
    ◦ Maintain posture and control throughout.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens the posterior deltoids, rhomboids, and middle trapezius
• Encourages better shoulder retraction and posture
• Beneficial for correcting rounded shoulders and improving shoulder stability
videoDescription: This video demonstrates shoulder horizontal abduction, which strengthens the posterior shoulder muscles. Start with arms extended in front of you at shoulder height, palms facing in. Open your arms wide like you’re making a “T” with your body, squeezing your shoulder blades together. Control the movement back to the start. Maintain a tall spine and avoid arching your low back.

title: Shoulder Horizontal Adduction
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand tall or sit upright with feet flat on the floor.
• Engage your core and maintain neutral spine alignment.
• Raise both arms out to your sides at shoulder height (forming a "T" position), palms facing forward or slightly inward.
• Keep a slight bend in your elbows.
Movement:
1. Begin the Adduction:
    ◦ Bring your arms inward across your chest in a controlled arc, as if giving a hug.
    ◦ Keep your arms parallel to the floor and lead with your elbows (not your wrists).
    ◦ Try to bring your hands or elbows close together in front of your chest, squeezing your chest muscles.
2. Return to Start:
    ◦ Slowly reverse the motion, opening your arms back out to shoulder level.
    ◦ Do not allow your back to arch or your shoulders to shrug.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Activates the pectoralis major, anterior deltoids, and serratus anterior
• Reinforces control of scapular movement and chest strength
• Supports shoulder joint mobility and postural alignment when paired with horizontal abduction
videoDescription: In this video, you’ll learn shoulder horizontal adduction to target the front of the shoulders and chest. Begin with arms opened out to the side at shoulder height, elbows slightly bent. Bring your arms toward the center of your body until your hands nearly meet in front of your chest. Squeeze through the chest, then slowly return. Keep the shoulders relaxed and avoid elevating them.

title: Shoulder Internal Rotation
instructions:
Setup / Posture:
• Stand tall or sit upright with feet flat on the ground.
• Maintain a neutral spine, engage your core, and keep your shoulders relaxed (not shrugged).
• Start with your elbow bent at 90 degrees, upper arm close to your torso, and forearm pointing straight forward (parallel to the floor).
• This can be performed with or without resistance (e.g., cable machine, resistance band, or light dumbbell).
Movement:
1. Begin the Rotation:
    ◦ Keeping your elbow tucked at your side, slowly rotate your forearm inward across your body.
    ◦ Your forearm should move toward your belly or the centerline of your body.
    ◦ Focus on moving only at the shoulder joint—avoid shifting your torso or letting the elbow drift.
2. Return to Start:
    ◦ Slowly reverse the motion, rotating your forearm back out to the starting position.
    ◦ Maintain control throughout the movement, especially when returning.
Reps / Sets:
• Perform 10–12 reps per arm
• Complete 2–3 sets
• Rest 30–60 seconds between sets
Focus:
• Strengthens the subscapularis (one of the rotator cuff muscles)
• Helps restore balance in the rotator cuff
• Crucial for clients with shoulder instability or postural imbalances like forward shoulders
videoDescription: This video shows how to perform shoulder internal rotation to strengthen the muscles on the front of the shoulder and rotator cuff. Begin with your elbow bent at 90 degrees, tucked close to your side, and forearm pointing straight ahead. Rotate your forearm inward across your body while keeping your elbow at your side. Pause briefly, then return with control. Maintain upright posture and avoid shrugging your shoulders.

title: SMR: Adductors
instructions:
Setup
• Lie face down and prop yourself on your forearms.
• Open one leg out to the side in a “frog” position (knee bent ~90°).
• Place the foam roller under the inner thigh of that leg, starting near the upper inner thigh (closer to the groin but not on it).
• Use your arms and opposite leg to control how much pressure you apply.
Action / How to Perform
1. Slowly roll along the inner thigh from upper inner thigh toward just above the knee (stay on the muscle, avoid the knee joint).
2. Move slowly and scan for tender/tight points.
3. When you find a tender spot, pause and hold pressure there.
4. While holding, gently rock the leg a few inches forward/back or slowly straighten and re-bend the knee (small range) 5–10 times.
5. Continue rolling and slightly adjust angle to cover both:

    ◦ More front-inner thigh, and
    ◦ More back-inner thigh.
Duration (Typical NASM Range)
• 30–90 seconds per tender spot, or about 1–2 minutes per inner thigh.
Coaching Cues
• “Go slow—inner thigh is sensitive; let it melt.”
• “Breathe out and relax your hips.”
• “Pressure should feel intense but tolerable—never sharp.”
• “Stay off the groin and off the knee joint.”
Common Mistakes
• Rolling too close into the groin (uncomfortable and not the target).
• Rolling directly onto the inside of the knee.
• Going too hard too soon and tensing the hips/glutes.
• Moving too fast and not holding on trigger points.
Modifications / Progressions
• Easier: Use less bodyweight (support more with arms/opposite leg) or use a softer roller.
• Harder: Shift more weight onto the working leg or use a firmer roller.
• Targeted (advanced): Pause and add small controlled leg rocks for deeper release.
Safety Notes
• Stop if you feel sharp pain, numbness, tingling, or radiating symptoms.
• Use caution with recent groin strains, hip pain, or acute inflammation—reduce pressure and avoid aggressive rolling.

title: SMR: Calves (Gastrocnemius/Soleus)
instructions:
Setup
• Sit on the floor with legs extended.
• Place a foam roller under one calf (start just above the Achilles, below the knee).
• Support your body with your hands behind you.
• Cross the other leg on top of the working leg to increase pressure (optional).
• Keep toes relaxed; ankle can move freely.
Action / How to Perform
1. Shift your weight onto the roller and slowly roll along the calf from above the Achilles to just below the knee.
2. Move at a controlled pace (think slow and steady, not fast).
3. When you find a tender/“tight” spot, pause and hold pressure on that point.
4. While holding, gently flex and point your ankle (toes up/toes down) 5–10 times to help the tissue release.
5. Continue scanning the calf:

    ◦ Roll the inner calf by slightly rotating the leg inward.
    ◦ Roll the outer calf by slightly rotating the leg outward.
Duration (Typical NASM Range)
• 30–90 seconds per tender spot, or about 1–2 minutes per calf total.
Coaching Cues
• “Move slow—let the roller do the work.”
• “Breathe normally; exhale as you settle into a tight spot.”
• “Keep pressure ‘uncomfortable but tolerable’—not sharp pain.”
• “Avoid rolling directly on the back of the knee.”
Common Mistakes
• Rolling too fast and skipping tight areas.
• Holding your breath or tensing the shoulders.
• Placing the roller on the knee joint or pressing into the back of the knee.
• Using so much pressure that pain causes you to brace hard or cramp.
Modifications / Progressions
• Easier: Keep the other foot on the floor (no leg cross) to reduce pressure.
• Harder: Cross the other leg on top or use a firmer roller / lacrosse ball (advanced).
Safety Notes
• Stop if you feel sharp pain, numbness, tingling, or symptoms that radiate.
• Use extra caution if you have recent calf strains, blood clot history/DVT risk, or acute swelling—refer to a clinician if unsure.

title: SMR: Hamstrings
instructions:
Setup
• Sit on the floor with legs extended.
• Place a foam roller under one hamstring (back of thigh), starting just above the back of the knee.
• Support your body with your hands behind you.
• To increase pressure, cross the other leg on top of the working leg (optional).
• Keep the working leg relaxed; toes can point up naturally.
Action / How to Perform
1. Shift your weight onto the roller and slowly roll along the hamstring from just above the back of the knee to just below the glute (avoid sitting directly on the sit bone).
2. Move at a controlled pace—slow scan for tender/tight points.
3. When you find a tender spot, pause and hold pressure there.
4. While holding, gently bend and straighten the knee 5–10 times (small, controlled range).
5. Continue scanning the hamstring by changing angle slightly to cover:

    ◦ Inner hamstring (rotate the leg slightly outward),
    ◦ Outer hamstring (rotate the leg slightly inward).
Duration (Typical NASM Range)
• 30–90 seconds per tender spot, or about 1–2 minutes per hamstring.
Coaching Cues
• “Slow down—tight spots show up when you move slowly.”
• “Breathe out as you hold pressure.”
• “Keep pressure uncomfortable-but-tolerable, not sharp.”
• “Stay off joints—avoid the back of the knee.”
Common Mistakes
• Rolling too fast and not pausing on tender points.
• Rolling directly into the back of the knee (joint/nerve area).
• Using too much pressure and bracing hard through the shoulders/neck.
• Holding your breath instead of relaxing into the roller.
Modifications / Progressions
• Easier: Keep the other foot on the floor (no leg cross) and unload weight with your hands.
• Harder: Cross the other leg on top or use a firmer roller.
• Targeted (advanced): Pause and add gentle knee flex/extend to increase release.
Safety Notes
• Stop if you feel sharp pain, numbness, tingling, or radiating symptoms down the leg.
• Use caution with recent hamstring strains or bruising—avoid aggressive pressure until healed.

title: SMR: Peroneals
instructions:
Setup
• Sit on the floor and position yourself on your side.
• Place a foam roller under the outside of your lower leg (between the ankle and just below the knee).
• Use your hands and top leg for support and to control pressure:

    ◦ Keep the top foot on the floor in front of you for balance, or
    ◦ Stack legs to increase pressure (optional/advanced).
• Start near the upper outer calf and work down toward the ankle.
Action / How to Perform
1. Shift weight onto the roller and slowly roll along the outside of the lower leg from just below the knee to above the ankle.
2. Move at a controlled pace—slow scan for tender/tight points.
3. When you find a tender spot, pause and hold pressure there.
4. While holding, gently move the ankle:

    ◦ Inversion/Eversion (sole in / sole out) 5–10 times, or
    ◦ Flex/point (toes up/down) 5–10 times.
5. Continue rolling and slightly adjust your body angle to cover:

    ◦ More front-lateral (closer to the shin), and
    ◦ More back-lateral (closer to the calf).
Duration (Typical NASM Range)
• 30–90 seconds per tender spot, or about 1–2 minutes per side.
Coaching Cues
• “Go slow—tiny movements find the real tight spots.”
• “Stay on the muscle, not the bone.”
• “Breathe and let the pressure soften over time.”
• “Keep it uncomfortable-but-tolerable, not sharp.”
Common Mistakes
• Rolling directly on the shin bone (tibia) instead of the outer muscle.
• Pressing too hard too soon, causing you to tense or cramp.
• Rolling onto the ankle bones or the side of the knee joint.
• Moving too fast and missing trigger points.
Modifications / Progressions
• Easier: Keep more weight in your hands and top foot to reduce pressure.
• Harder: Stack legs or use a firmer roller.
• Targeted (advanced): Use a lacrosse ball for smaller, precise areas (go lighter than you think).
Safety Notes
• Stop if you feel sharp pain, numbness, tingling, or pain that radiates into the foot.
• Use caution with recent ankle sprains, acute inflammation, or swelling—if symptoms worsen, pause and reassess.

title: SMR: Quadriceps
instructions:
Setup
• Lie face down (prone) and place a foam roller under one quad (front of thigh), starting just above the knee.
• Support your upper body on your forearms (plank-like position).
• Keep core lightly braced and hips level.
• To increase pressure, you can:

    ◦ Shift more body weight onto the working leg, or
    ◦ Stack the other leg on top (advanced), if comfortable.
Action / How to Perform
1. Slowly roll along the quad from just above the knee to the front of the hip (stay on the muscle belly).
2. Move at a controlled pace—scan for tender/tight areas.
3. When you find a tender spot, pause and hold pressure there.
4. While holding, gently bend and straighten the knee 5–10 times (small, controlled range).
5. Adjust your body angle to cover the full quad:

    ◦ Rotate slightly inward to target outer quad (vastus lateralis).
    ◦ Rotate slightly outward to target inner quad (vastus medialis).
Duration (Typical NASM Range)
• 30–90 seconds per tender spot, or about 1–2 minutes per quad.
Coaching Cues
• “Go slow—this is tissue work, not cardio.”
• “Keep ribs down and glutes relaxed.”
• “Breathe out as you settle into a tight spot.”
• “Stay on the muscle—avoid rolling directly on bones/joints.”
Common Mistakes
• Rolling too fast and skipping tender points.
• Rolling directly on the kneecap or grinding into the knee joint.
• Letting hips twist or lower back sag (losing core control).
• Using too much pressure and tensing/holding breath.
Modifications / Progressions
• Easier: Roll both quads at once (less pressure per leg) or support more weight through forearms.
• Harder: Shift more weight onto one leg or use a firmer roller.
• Targeted (advanced): Pause on tender spots and add slow knee flex/extend.
Safety Notes
• Stop if you feel sharp pain, numbness, tingling, or pain that radiates.
• Use caution with recent quad strains, acute inflammation, or knee pain—reduce pressure and avoid the joint area.

title: Thoracic Extension
instructions:
Setup / Posture:

• Sit upright on a bench or chair with feet flat

• Place hands behind your head or across your chest

• Keep your spine tall and neck in neutral position
Movement:

• Gently arch through the upper back (thoracic spine), lifting your chest toward the ceiling

• Avoid overextending the lower back — focus the movement in the upper-mid back

• Hold for 1–2 seconds at end range, then return to neutral
Reps / Sets:

• Perform 8–12 reps

• Complete 2–3 sets

• Rest as needed
Focus:

• Improves thoracic extension mobility and posture

• Relieves tension caused by excessive flexion (slouching)

• Prepares the spine for overhead and full-body movements
videoDescription: This movement opens the chest and extends the mid-back, counteracting the effects of slouching or poor desk posture. It’s key for improving thoracic mobility and posture.

title: Thoracic Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture:

• Sit or stand tall with feet hip-width apart

• Hands can cross over the chest or reach forward

• Engage the core gently and keep the neck neutral
Movement:

• Slowly round the upper back by tucking your chin slightly and drawing your chest inward

• Think about bringing your ribcage closer to your pelvis

• Allow the shoulders to move slightly forward without shrugging

• Return to an upright position by reversing the movement with control
Reps / Sets:

• Perform 8–12 reps

• Complete 2–3 sets

• Rest as needed
Focus:

• Encourages mobility and articulation in the thoracic spine

• Reduces excessive extension and postural tension

• Useful for correcting forward head and rounded shoulder patterns
videoDescription: This movement helps round the upper back gently, increasing spinal mobility and releasing tension from tight thoracic extensor muscles. It’s helpful for clients with stiffness, poor posture, or upper-crossed syndrome.

title: Thoracic Lateral Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture:

• Sit or stand with feet hip-width apart and spine upright

• Arms can rest at your sides or one arm can reach overhead

• Keep your hips level and avoid leaning forward or backward
Movement:

• Slowly bend your torso to the right side, reaching toward your hip or extending the opposite arm overhead

• Keep the movement isolated to the thoracic spine — avoid crunching the neck or collapsing the ribs forward

• Return to center with control, then repeat on the left
Reps / Sets:

• Perform 8–10 reps per side

• Complete 2–3 sets

• Rest briefly between sets
Focus:

• Enhances lateral mobility in the thoracic spine

• Relieves stiffness caused by static posture

• Supports breathing mechanics and rib mobility
videoDescription: Thoracic lateral flexion improves side-bending mobility in the upper and mid-back, often restricted by muscle tightness or prolonged sitting. It promotes postural balance and functional range of motion.

title: Thoracic Rotation
instructions:
Setup / Posture:

• Sit on a bench or chair with feet flat and spine tall

• Cross your arms over your chest or place hands on opposite shoulders

• Keep your hips facing forward and core gently engaged
Movement:

• Slowly rotate your torso to the right, initiating the movement from the ribcage

• Keep your head in line with your spine — avoid leading with your neck

• Pause briefly at end range, then return to center

• Repeat to the left side with control
Reps / Sets:

• Perform 8–10 reps per side

• Complete 2–3 sets

• Rest briefly between sets
Focus:

• Encourages mobility and coordination through the thoracic spine

• Reduces compensations in the lumbar spine and shoulders

• Supports posture and rotational performance in daily life
videoDescription: This movement helps improve rotational mobility in the mid-back, which is often limited by sedentary posture. It’s key for improving spinal health, shoulder mechanics, and injury prevention.

title: Thumb Extension
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit or stand comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Rest your forearm on a table or hold your hand out in front of you.
• Start with your hand open and fingers relaxed.
• Keep your wrist neutral (not bent up or down).
Movement
1. Start with your thumb relaxed near the side of your hand.
2. Slowly move your thumb away from your palm—like you’re opening space between your thumb and index finger.
3. Pause 1–2 seconds at the end range without forcing.
4. Return to the start position with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per hand
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Move from the thumb—keep the wrist still.
• Keep the motion controlled and pain-free.
• You should feel gentle activation at the base of the thumb (not sharp pain).
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Wrist moves to “cheat” → Rest forearm on a table; keep wrist neutral.
• Thumb collapses or curls → “Keep thumb long; move it away from the palm.”
• Pain at base of thumb → Reduce range and slow down; stop if sharp pain.
videoDescription: Thumb extension is the motion of moving your thumb away from your palm (as if giving a “thumbs up” or opening your hand for a wide grip). This supports daily tasks like gripping larger objects, holding a cup, texting, lifting, and stabilizing the hand—especially if your thumb feels stiff from overuse.

title: Thumb Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit or stand comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Rest your forearm on a table or hold your hand out in front of you.
• Start with your hand open and fingers relaxed.
• Keep your wrist neutral (not bent up or down).
Movement
1. Start with your thumb relaxed away from the palm.
2. Slowly move your thumb across your palm, aiming toward the base of your pinky side (don’t force it).
3. Pause 1–2 seconds at end range.
4. Return to the start position with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per hand
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Keep the movement in the thumb (not the wrist).
• Move slowly and pain-free—avoid forcing range.
• Feel gentle activation through the thumb and palm, not sharp pain.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Wrist bends to help → Rest forearm on table; keep wrist neutral.
• Thumb curls/tucks → “Keep thumb long; glide across the palm.”
• Pinching pain at base of thumb → Reduce range and slow down; stop if sharp pain.
videoDescription: Thumb flexion is the motion of bringing your thumb across your palm (toward the base of the pinky side). This supports everyday tasks like gripping, holding objects, texting, buttoning, opening containers, and fine motor control, especially if your thumb feels stiff or weak.

title: Thumb Opposition
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit or stand comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Rest your forearm on a table or hold your hand out in front of you.
• Start with your hand open and fingers relaxed.
• Keep your wrist neutral (not bent up or down).
Movement
1. Touch the tip of your thumb to the tip of your index finger.
2. Return to an open hand.
3. Repeat with the middle finger, then ring finger, then pinky.
4. Keep each touch gentle and controlled—avoid pressing hard.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 rounds per hand (index → middle → ring → pinky)
• Option: 1–2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth fingertip touches
Focus
• Keep the thumb long and controlled (don’t collapse the thumb joint).
• Touch fingertip to fingertip—avoid flattening the fingers.
• Smooth movement; no rushing.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Wrist moving → Rest forearm on table; keep wrist neutral.
• Thumb joint collapsing → “Keep thumb tall; touch with the tip.”
• Pressing too hard → “Light touch; this is control and coordination.”
videoDescription: Thumb opposition is the motion of bringing your thumb to touch your fingertips. It’s a key movement for hand function and coordination, supporting tasks like gripping, writing, typing, opening containers, buttoning, and picking up small objects

title: Wrist Abduction
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Rest your forearm on a table with your hand hanging slightly off the edge or place your forearm on your thigh.
• Palm facing down (or thumb-up position is fine—just stay consistent).
• Keep your forearm still and your wrist neutral to start.
Movement
1. Keeping your forearm still, slowly move your hand toward the thumb side (like waving toward your thumb).
2. Pause 1–2 seconds at the end range.
3. Return to center with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per side
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Movement comes from the wrist (not the elbow/shoulder).
• Keep the motion small and controlled—no snapping.
• Stay pain-free; mild stretch is okay, sharp pain is not.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Forearm lifting or sliding → Anchor forearm on the table/thigh.
• Turning the hand instead of moving side-to-side → “Slide toward the thumb, don’t rotate.”
• Too much range causing pain → Reduce range and slow down.
videoDescription: Wrist abduction (radial deviation) is the motion of moving your hand toward the thumb side. This supports daily tasks like lifting/carrying, typing, gripping, pouring, and reaching, and helps improve wrist control—especially if your wrists feel stiff from repetitive hand use.

title: Wrist Adduction
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Rest your forearm on a table with your hand hanging slightly off the edge or place your forearm on your thigh.
• Palm facing down (or thumb-up position is fine—stay consistent).
• Keep your forearm still and start with your wrist neutral.
Movement
1. Keeping your forearm still, slowly move your hand toward the pinky side (side-to-side at the wrist).
2. Pause 1–2 seconds at the end range.
3. Return to center with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per side
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Move from the wrist—avoid elbow/shoulder movement.
• Smooth, controlled motion—no snapping.
• Stay pain-free; reduce range if you feel sharp discomfort.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Forearm moving → Anchor forearm on the table/thigh.
• Rotating instead of sliding → “Move side-to-side, don’t twist.”
• Pain at end range → Decrease range and slow down.
videoDescription: Wrist adduction (ulnar deviation) is the motion of moving your hand toward the pinky side. This supports daily tasks like gripping, carrying, lifting, typing, using tools, and stabilizing the wrist during workouts and work tasks. It’s a simple drill to improve wrist control and mobility.

title: Wrist Extension
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Rest your forearm on a table with your hand hanging slightly off the edge or place your forearm on your thigh.
• Keep your forearm anchored and start with your wrist neutral.
• Fingers relaxed (not clenched).
Movement
1. Keeping your forearm still, slowly bend your wrist so your hand moves upward (back of hand toward forearm).
2. Pause 1–2 seconds at the end range.
3. Return to neutral with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per side
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Move from the wrist only (no elbow/shoulder movement).
• Keep the motion smooth—no snapping.
• Stay pain-free; reduce range if you feel sharp discomfort.
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Forearm shifts/moves → Anchor forearm on the table/thigh.
• Finger tension/clenching → “Relax the hand; move only the wrist.”
• Pinching pain → Reduce range and slow down; stop if sharp pain.
videoDescription: Wrist extension is the motion of bending your wrist so the back of your hand moves toward your forearm (like making a “stop” hand). This supports daily tasks like pushing up from a chair, getting off the floor, typing, gripping, and weight-bearing exercises (planks, push-ups), and helps improve wrist control and mobility.

title: Wrist Flexion
instructions:
Setup / Posture
• Sit comfortably with shoulders relaxed.
• Rest your forearm on a table with your hand hanging slightly off the edge or place your forearm on your thigh.
• Palm facing down to start (or palm-up is fine—just keep the forearm still).
• Keep your forearm anchored and wrist neutral.
Movement
1. Keeping your forearm still, slowly bend your wrist so your hand moves downward (palm toward forearm).
2. Pause 1–2 seconds at the end range.
3. Return to neutral with control.
Reps / Sets
• 2–3 sets of 10–15 reps per side
• Option: 2 sets of 20–30 seconds of smooth reps
Focus
• Move from the wrist only (no elbow/shoulder movement).
• Smooth, controlled motion—avoid snapping.
• Keep fingers relaxed (don’t clench a fist unless instructed).
Common mistakes + quick fixes
• Forearm lifts/moves → Anchor forearm on the table/thigh.
• Gripping/clenching → “Relax your fingers; move only the wrist.”
• Pain at end range → Reduce range and slow down.
videoDescription: Wrist flexion is the motion of bending your wrist so your palm moves toward your forearm. This supports daily tasks like gripping, carrying, typing, lifting, and pushing/pulling, and helps improve wrist control—especially if your wrists feel stiff from repetitive hand use.
